There is a particular comfort in unfinished things. A half-read novel slipping between the couch cushions, a sweater with one sleeve knitted and the other still lying in a basket, a letter that begins "Dear Margaret" and then stalls. We tend to treat completion as the goal, but unfinished things keep a door open. They hold a version of ourselves that intended something and hasn't yet been disappointed.

I think about this when I walk past old buildings with scaffolding that has stood for years, or when I notice a garden bed that was supposed to be planted in spring and is now a tangle of volunteer dandelions. Nothing about these scenes is tragic. They are simply in the middle of a sentence.

Perhaps the discomfort we feel toward unfinished work comes from a narrow idea of what a life should look like, as if it were a ledger that must balance by the end. But most meaningful things I can name were never finished in any clean sense. Friendships keep changing shape. Languages are never fully learned. The stories we tell about our grandparents grow more complicated the longer we live, not less.

There's a kind of honesty in leaving things open. It admits that we don't know how it ends, and that not knowing is part of what makes attention worth paying. A finished thing asks nothing more of us. An unfinished one invites us back.

So maybe I'll leave a few things unfinished on purpose this week: a chapter I'm not ready to close, a conversation I'll pick up tomorrow, a question I don't need to answer yet. The sweater can wait in its basket. It has earned the right to stay a little incomplete.
